slides.say: For every positive integer x, the double bracket of x is the number of times five appears in the prime factorization of x. For example, fifty is two times five times five, it has two fives, so the double bracket of fifty is two. Which of the following must be true?
Operations meet prime numbers. [short pause] We'll solve it two ways, plugging in numbers, and then by understanding.
[short pause] A definition in words is easy to misread, so a few examples first. Fifty has two fives. Seventy-five is three times five times five, two fives as well. And seven has no fives, zero.

Now plug in the simplest value, x is one, no fives at all. Choice number one, five has one five, and one squared has none. One against zero. Out. Choice number two, six has none, but zero plus one is one. Out. Choice number three, one against five times zero. Out.
at: zero plus one is one. Out

slides.say: Choice number four, five has one five, and zero plus one is one. True. Three are out, so choice number four is our answer. One is a risky number, it can make a false rule look true, but here three failed and one survived.

[pause] Now why. What's different? We reason about the factors instead of trying numbers. Choice number two adds five, and adding says nothing about the factors. Choice number one squares x, and squaring doubles the number of fives.
Choice number three multiplies the count by five. x is five cubed, times five gives four fives, not fifteen.

And choice number four. Multiply x by five, and you add exactly one more five to its factors. So the count goes up by exactly one, every time. Choice number four. [pause] Okay. I'll see you in the next question.
